title: Flood victim, 95, lived in Wetherspoons until she died after her home was destroyed
summary: Jean Powell kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow burst its banks.
text: Monmouth flood victim died before she could return home - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat Wales Wales Politics Wales Business North West North East Mid South West South East Cymru Local News Flood victim, 95, lived in Wetherspoons until she died after her home was destroyed Image source, Wyn Smith Image caption, Jean Powell was temporarily staying in one of Monmouth Wetherspoons' guest rooms while her flat was being refurbished after it was flooded a year ago By Peter Shuttleworth , Reporting from Monmouth and Lucy Vladev , BBC Wales Published 12 November 2026 Updated 7 hours ago When neighbours hammered on Jean Powell's door and evacuated her to safety because the nearby river had burst its banks and swamped her town, little did she know she would never return home. Jean sought a 10-month refuge at her local Wetherspoons but kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow hit 18-times its normal level in south Wales in November 2025 . But the 95-year-old never got to go back home and died in September - one of those who suffered a personal toll from the effects of being flooded. "Jean used to say, when am I going home?" said friend and neighbour Wyn Smith. "All she wanted to do was come back home and we couldn't fulfil that." Figure caption, The BBC report from last year when Monmouth town centre was hit by severe flooding after Storm Claudia Jean was forced out of her home when the river hit record levels in the early hours of 15 November as a major incident was declared after almost a month's worth of rain fell in 24 hours. It has officially been described as a one-in-75-year event when the river flooded more than 400 properties in the Welsh town during Storm Claudia - and overwhelmed the defences that were built 35 years ago to protect the centre of town. Jean, like many in the small town near the Wales and England border, was rescued and after sleeping the night on her neighbour's chair sought temporary sanctuary in Monmouth's Wetherspoons as she had no close family to look after her. "She was happy in the beginning because she was in town where she wanted to be," recalled Wyn, who visited her friend most days who was staying in one of The Kings Head's hotel rooms. "The Wetherspoons staff were brilliant with Jean, they'd take her food and really looked after her." Image caption, Wyn Smith helped her neighbours to safety when floodwaters swamped their block of flats in Monmouth, and now she's awaiting their return as renovations near the end "We never thought she'd be there that long," said Wyn. "It's nobody's fault, it took a long time to dry her home out. It had to be done properly." Residents have been with family, some are in rented accommodation, some have been in an Airbnb while another is in a care home. Their story is typical of many in Monmouth who have been out of their home since Claudia struck - and that trauma and anxiety from the devastation of 12 months ago is never far from the surface. "Some had been through the war and they said it upset them more than that. It was just awful," said Wyn. Image source, Gillian Haycock Image caption, This was how ground floor residents in Jean's Chippenham Court retirement complex found their flats after Storm Claudia "But unfortunately it could happen again. There's that fear. If they see water coming, it'll freak them out. They need to feel at home and not worry about the weather." The Met Office estimates that with current levels of global warming, record-breaking wet winters have gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events . Wales' environmental body has warned long-range forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of wetter, windier weather than usual this winter, with Natural Resources Wales (NRW) saying people should prepare for "the unthinkable" . Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Monmouth's main shopping street was submerged after the nearby River Monnow burst its banks as it reached record levels during Storm Claudia Apart from three nights at the local Premier Inn over Christmas when Wetherspoons was shut - where Jean had sandwiches from the nearby petrol station for Christmas dinner because she wanted to "remain independent" - she stayed above the pub in the town's main square for almost 10 months. "As time went on, living in one room was awful for her," recalled Wyn, 70. "When Jean got ill, it wasn't a place for her to live. Her health deteriorated and she didn't come back home, which is sad." Jean's death will be acutely felt when the first displaced residents return to the Chippenham Court retirement complex she called home following its £1m refurbishment in the next few weeks. Figure caption, Emily Frost recalls how she had to wake her two boys in the middle of the night and evacuate their family home before it was flooded during Storm Claudia One in seven properties in Wales are at risk of flooding, including the Frost household on the other side of Monmouth where Emily says she and her young family will never recover from being evacuated on a lifeboat last year. The mum-of-two breaks down as she recalls being woken by the coastguard telling her she's got five minutes to evacuate her family as the floodwaters surged towards her end-of-terrace cottage. "Opening the door, I completely freaked out to the lifeguard," Emily told the BBC. "They were waist deep in water and said our house was at risk.
